finite_default_domain.definition: All ordered selections of 3 distinct symbols from 5: 5×4×3 = 60.
finite_default_domain.scope: Default native parameter distribution only; finite input count is not inflated by repeated sampling.

provenance: Opus 5.5 subscription CLI draft with host review/repairs, source restrictions and execution verification.

draft_notes.explanation: The original grid is three 3x3 panels laid side by side. Each panel holds a symbol drawn in colour 5 on colour 0, and the output fills each panel solid with the colour that symbol stands for. The factory turns the five original symbol masks (top row, bottom row, ring, anti-diagonal, centre dot) into the visible orientation: it reverses the rows if d4>=4, then rotates clockwise d4%4 times. It maps each symbol's colour (6,1,3,9,4) through the palette. Applying D4 to the whole grid applies the same D4 to each 3x3 block, so these transformed masks are exactly what will appear in the visible panels. Odd rotations turn the 3x9 grid into 9x3, so the panels are then stacked vertically. The emitted program cuts the visible grid into square panels along its long axis, using the panel size of the short side. It marks pixels equal to palette[5] in each panel, looks the mask up in the specialized table, and paints the panel solid with the matching palette colour. Demonstration pairs can add entries to the table but never override the built-in ones. If a mask is unknown, the program falls back to the nearest symbol by Hamming distance.
draft_notes.limitations: This has not been run or tested. It assumes the constructor's domain: three 3x3 panels along the long axis, foreground palette[5], and the five fixed symbols. If a panel mask is not in the table and no demo supplies it, the program uses the nearest-match fallback, which may be wrong. The fixtures were consistent with one uniform rule; no contradictions were found.
